column1: # The Advent calendar (/advent, scripts/tools/make-advent.js): day (1-24), title, a line taken from the linked page's
# own text (at most 170 characters), address (/encyclopedia/<slug> or /songs/<slug>). Chosen and read by hand: a
# festival of the dark season, a carol, or something that happened on that day; nothing grim (children open these doors).

column3: The season of waiting before Christmas opens the church's year. Its name comes from the Latin adventus, "coming".
In ancient Rome December was the month of Saturn's festival, with a public banquet, gifts and masters serving their slaves at table.
In China the winter solstice is a festival: families gather to eat tangyuan, balls of glutinous rice that stand for reunion.
On the longest night of the year, families in Iran gather to eat, read the poems of Hafez and share pomegranates and watermelons.
Tonight is St. Nicholas' Eve, when gifts are given in the Netherlands. Sinterklaas arrives by steamboat and rides a white horse.
A 4th-century bishop of Myra, patron of sailors and children. In Belgium and nearby lands his gifts come this morning.
An eight-day Jewish festival, usually in December, when one more candle or lamp is lit each night.
A Hebrew hymn sung on Hanukkah after the candles are lit, written in the 13th century or a little earlier.
The custom grew up in Germany and Livonia. Records tell of a tree in the Cathedral of Strasbourg in 1539.
Francis of Assisi is said to have staged the first one at Christmas 1223, in a cave near Greccio.
A Latin Christmas song for children's voices, first printed in a Finnish school songbook in 1582.
Canada's oldest Christmas song, written around 1642 in the language of the Wendat (Huron) people.
A festival of light. In the legend, Lucy wore a wreath of candles on her head to light her way.
On this day in 1911 Roald Amundsen and four companions became the first people to reach the South Pole.
Among the Slavs, singers called koledari go from house to house on Christmas Eve and receive gifts for their carols.
An English custom of Christmastide: a hot spiced drink, and songs sung from door to door.
On this day in 1903 Orville Wright flew the Wright Flyer for 12 seconds, the first of four flights that day.
The ballet set on Christmas Eve was first performed on this day in 1892, in Saint Petersburg.
Charles Dickens's story of the miser Scrooge was published on this day in 1843 and sold out by Christmas Eve.
An old English folk carol. The tune sung today was written down from a woman's singing in 1909.
The shortest day of the year in the north. Stonehenge and Newgrange are aligned with its sunrise or sunset.
The winter festival of the old Germanic peoples. Its name still means Christmas in English and other northern languages.
A widely sung carol from Italy, written in 1744 by a Neapolitan priest and often played on the zampogna, a big bagpipe.
First sung with a guitar in a village church in Austria on Christmas Eve 1818, and now sung in about 300 languages.
